basics.title: Frequency and probability are not the same thing

frequency.def: How many times something has happened over a specific number of past matches. It's a count, not a prediction: ‘over 2.5 happened in 13 of the last 20 matches’ is frequency.

modelProbability.def: An estimate made with a statistical model that takes each team's strength into account, not just a count: for the result percentages, the average of our own Elo and Dixon-Coles. It is still an estimate, not a fact.

oneXTwo.def: Market on the full-time result: 1 (home win), X (draw) or 2 (away win).

btts.def: Whether both teams score at least one goal in the match, yes or no.

overUnder.def: Whether the match ends with more than 2.5 goals in total (over) or with 2.5 or fewer (under).

asianHandicap.def: A 1X2 market with a goal advantage or disadvantage applied beforehand to one of the teams, to even out the chances.

halfTime.def: The score at the end of the first half, not the final result.

streak.def: Consecutive matches, counting back from the most recent, in which a team (or a referee) has met a condition: winning, scoring, over 8.5 corners... It describes what has happened, not what will happen.

rarity.def: How hard it would be to see that streak by pure chance if the team were just any side in the league: the league's usual rate for that event, raised to the power of the streak's length. Winning 8 in a row where 40% of matches are won: 0.40<sup>8</sup> ≈ 1 in 1,500, very rare. A streak of 9 of something that happens 90% of the time: 0.90<sup>9</sup> ≈ 1 in 3, not rare at all. It isn't the probability of the streak continuing: it assumes independent matches and an average team, and a team with a distinctive style (shooting a lot, committing lots of fouls) can have extremely rare streaks without them being a surprise.

implied.def: The probability that odds ‘assume’ if you take them at face value: 1 ÷ odds. Odds of 2.00 imply 50%.

fair.def: The odds that would correspond exactly to the model's probability, with no bookmaker margin: 1 ÷ model probability. They're a reference for comparison, not odds you'll necessarily find anywhere.

margin.def: How many points it is right above (+) or below (−) what the market expected, using its probability without the bookmaker's margin. It matters more than the hit rate: always picking what the market sees as most likely is also right a lot, and loses money. Each league's bars are its 95% range: it comes from repeating the calculation 2000 times with matches drawn at random from the same ones; if a bar crosses 0, that edge cannot be told apart from luck.

test.def: 22/23 to 24/25: in the Premier League and LaLiga, with the model retrained each season using only earlier ones; in LaLiga Hypermotion and Serie A, with the current model, which never saw those leagues. 25/26 and 26/27: the selections in the history, made with a model trained only on earlier seasons and with the thresholds set before seeing those matches. Missed selections are never removed from the list or the figures.

rate.def: The share of predictions that came true. Only those made with the data available before each match count.

sample.def: How many predictions with a result are behind each figure. Below 100 there is a “little data” warning: a few more matches can move the hit rate quite a lot.

interval.def: Where the model's real hit rate almost certainly (95%) lies, given that number of predictions. The fewer the predictions, the wider it is. It is calculated with the Wilson method.

base.def: What each model is compared with: the market (who wins, double chance, High probability) or a simple rule without a model (predictor, duel, picks). Each card names the exact rule. Who wins: always the market favourite, the result with the lowest odds, without margin. Double chance: the most likely one according to the market. In these two, matches without stored odds do not count, for the model or for the baseline. Corner duel and predictor: the team with the higher average of that stat over its last 10 matches in that competition (or as many as it has, if fewer), using earlier matches only. If the two averages tie or a team has no history, the match stays out of the comparison. Likely picks: how often each event happens across the league, that is, how many times it happened in the matches played before that one, in that season and the previous one. If the pick is based on a team's home or away matches, only that venue counts. High probability: the probability the market gave before the match, without its margin.

edge.def: The hit rate minus the reference, in points: how much the model adds over it. Its range comes from repeating the calculation 2000 times with matches drawn at random from the same ones; if it includes 0, the edge cannot be told apart from luck.

side.def: Whether the team the predictor expected to get more shots, corners, fouls... was the one that got more. Matches with a tie in that stat do not count, and yellow cards only count with an appointed referee.

mae.def: How far, on average, what the predictor expected from a team was from what it really got. It is compared with what the league average would give: if the predictor is wrong by less, it adds something. It is its main measure; lower is better.

origin.term: Saved before the match / Calculated with earlier data
origin.def: Saved before the match: the prediction was saved before kick-off and has not been touched. Calculated with earlier data: it was calculated afterwards, but only with the matches played before, as if it had been made at the time.

uncalibrated.def: The Champions League was not part of these models' tests: its figures are shown, but they do not count in the totals.

repeat.def: Whether the order of teams or leagues in one season resembles the next one. It is measured with a correlation, from 0 (not at all) to 1 (the same): hardly at all below 0.2, a little up to 0.4, quite a lot up to 0.6 and a lot above that. If it repeats little, being at the top this season says little about the next.

ranking.def: Each row counts all the predictions from the matches the team plays in, including those about the opponent: in a match with 6 picks, all 6 count for both teams. It is in alphabetical order and every column sorts; below 20 predictions there is a “little data” warning. Opening a team shows its matches with each pick: ✓ came true, ✗ did not.
